issue: Can the First Step Act's prospective-only change to § 924(c) stacking (the anti-stacking amendment) be an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), either alone or through the Commission's policy statement U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)?

sides.position: The § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment cannot be an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction, because that would give the prospective-only amendment retroactive effect that Congress withheld. Under this view, U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) cannot be used to reach that result.
cases: United States v. Thacker, 4 F.4th 569 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Black, 131 F.4th 542 (7th Cir. 2025)
United States v. Andrews, 12 F.4th 255 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Rutherford, 120 F.4th 360 (3d Cir. 2024)
United States v. Austin, 125 F.4th 688 (5th Cir. 2025)
United States v. McCall, 56 F.4th 1048 (6th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Crandall, 25 F.4th 582 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Jenkins, 50 F.4th 1185 (D.C. Cir. 2022)

sides.position: The anti-stacking amendment can be an extraordinary and compelling reason, at least in the circumstances covered by U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6), so the sentencing court may consider it.
cases: United States v. Ruvalcaba, 26 F.4th 14 (1st Cir. 2022)
United States v. McCoy, 981 F.3d 271 (4th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Chen, 48 F.4th 1092 (9th Cir. 2022)
United States v. McGee, 992 F.3d 1035 (10th Cir. 2021)

this_court: The anti-stacking amendment cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction; the court follows Thacker and declines to treat § 1B1.13(b)(6) as overriding it. The concurrence would instead defer to the Commission's policy statement.
quote: We recognize Thacker's holding that § 924(c)'s anti-stacking amendment cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction is not consensus; the courts of appeals have split on the issue.
cite: United States v. Eural Black, 131 F.4th 542 (7th Cir. 2025)
